The derivation of the weak form takes a few lines. Its *meaning* takes longer to see.
This appendix answers three questions that the derivation leaves open:

1. **Where does the Poisson equation come from, and in what sense is $a(w, u)$ an
   energy?** (@sec-wf-conservation, @sec-wf-energy)
2. **Why multiply by a test function and integrate?** (@sec-wf-test)
3. **What exactly are trial and test functions, and what does Galerkin's method do with
   them?** (@sec-wf-spaces, @sec-wf-galerkin)

The answers fit together into one picture:

::: {.derivation}
$$
\begin{gathered}
\boxed{\text{conservation}}+\boxed{\text{constitutive law}}
\;\Longrightarrow\; (\mathrm{S}) \\[6pt]
(\mathrm{S})
\;\Longleftrightarrow\; (\mathrm{W})
\;\Longleftrightarrow\; \boxed{\text{minimum of an energy } \Pi} \\[6pt]
(\mathrm{W}) \;\xrightarrow{\;\text{restrict to } \mathcal S^h,\,\mathcal V^h\;}\;
(\mathrm{G})
\;\Longrightarrow\; \mathbf K\mathbf d=\mathbf F
\end{gathered}
$$
:::

The arrows before $(\mathrm{G})$ are equivalences: when the solution is smooth enough,
the strong form, the weak form, and the energy minimum all describe the same
boundary-value problem. The arrow to $(\mathrm{G})$ is different. **That is where
approximation enters.**

Every interactive plot on this page runs on the same small problem. Change its setup in
@sec-wf-setup and all of them update.

## The running example {#sec-wf-model}

A wall occupies $\Omega = \,]0, 1[$, in nondimensional units. Its left half has
conductivity $\kappa_1$ and its right half $\kappa_2$. Heat is generated inside it at the
rate $f(x)$ per unit volume, a heat flux $h$ is pushed into its left face, and a
thermostat holds its right face at the temperature $g$. This is the arrangement of the
[1D wall](Poisson1D_Heat.qmd), with one change: two materials.

($f$), and leaves through the thermostat on the right ($\Gamma_g$), which holds the face

::: {.panel-tabset}

### The 1D problem, used below

$$
(\mathrm{S})\qquad
\begin{aligned}
&-\left(\kappa\,u_{,x}\right)_{,x} = f && \text{on } ]0, 1[ \\
&u(1) = g && \Gamma_g = \{1\} \\
&-\kappa\,u_{,x}(0) = h && \Gamma_h = \{0\}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
(\mathrm{W})\qquad
\begin{aligned}
&\text{find } u \in \mathcal S \text{ such that, for all } w \in \mathcal V, \\
&\qquad \underbrace{\int_0^1 w_{,x}\,\kappa\,u_{,x}\,dx}_{a(w,\,u)}
= \underbrace{\int_0^1 w\,f\,dx + w(0)\,h}_{\ell(w)}
\end{aligned}
$$

with $\mathcal S = \{u \in H^1 : u(1) = g\}$ and
$\mathcal V = \{w \in H^1 : w(1) = 0\}$.

### The general problem

$$
(\mathrm{S})\qquad
-\nabla\cdot\left(\underline{\underline{K}}\nabla u\right) = f \;\text{ in } \Omega,
\qquad u = g \;\text{ on } \Gamma_g,
\qquad \left(\underline{\underline{K}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n} = h \;\text{ on } \Gamma_h
$$

$$
(\mathrm{W})\qquad
\int_\Omega \nabla w\cdot\underline{\underline{K}}\nabla u\;d\Omega
= \int_\Omega w\,f\;d\Omega + \int_{\Gamma_h} w\,h\;d\Gamma
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\int_\Omega w_{,i}K_{ij}u_{,j}\;d\Omega
= \int_\Omega w\,f\;d\Omega + \int_{\Gamma_h} w\,h\;d\Gamma
$$

Nothing below depends on the dimension. The 1D version keeps the pictures simple.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Sign convention used in these notes"}
The physical heat flux is $\underline q=-\underline{\underline K}\nabla u$ (in 1D,
$q = -\kappa u_{,x}$). Hughes' Neumann datum is $h=-\underline q\cdot\underline n
=\left(\underline{\underline K}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline n$, so positive $h$ means
heat entering the domain. At $x = 0$ the outward normal is $n = -1$, so the condition
reads $-\kappa u_{,x}(0) = h$, that is, $q(0) = h$: **$h$ is the heat entering the wall.**
:::

### Problem setup {#sec-wf-setup}

Every interactive plot below uses this setup.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof setup = Inputs.form({
  k1: Inputs.range([0.2, 3], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "κ₁ (left half)"}),
  k2: Inputs.range([0.2, 3], {value: 0.5, step: 0.05, label: "κ₂ (right half)"}),
  src: Inputs.radio(["uniform", "hot spot near x = 0.3", "none"], {value: "uniform", label: "source f(x)"}),
  f0: Inputs.range([0, 5], {value: 2, step: 0.1, label: "total source ∫f dx"}),
  h: Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 0.5, step: 0.1, label: "h (heat in at x = 0)"}),
  g: Inputs.range([-1, 1], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "g (temperature at x = 1)"})
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
// ---------- shared numerics: everything lives on a fine grid of N cells ----------
N = 2520
dx = 1 / N
xs = Array.from({length: N + 1}, (_, i) => i / N)
xm = Array.from({length: N}, (_, i) => (i + 0.5) / N)

P = {
  const {k1, k2, src, f0, h, g} = setup;
  const kap = x => (x < 0.5 ? k1 : k2);
  const s = 0.07;
  const f = src === "uniform" ? (x => f0)
          : src === "none" ? (x => 0)
          : (x => f0 * Math.exp(-(((x - 0.3) / s) ** 2)) / (s * Math.sqrt(Math.PI)));
  const kmid = xm.map(kap), fmid = xm.map(f);
  // the exact solution from the energy balance: q(x) = h + ∫_0^x f,  u' = -q/κ,  u(1) = g
  const q = new Array(N + 1); q[0] = h;
  for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) q[i + 1] = q[i] + fmid[i] * dx;
  const u = new Array(N + 1); u[N] = g;
  for (let i = N - 1; i >= 0; i--) u[i] = u[i + 1] + dx * 0.5 * (q[i] + q[i + 1]) / kmid[i];
  return {k1, k2, f0, h, g, src, kap, f, kmid, fmid, q, u};
}

// a(w,v) = ∫ w' κ v' dx
function aF(w, v, P) {
  let s = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) s += P.kmid[i] * (w[i + 1] - w[i]) * (v[i + 1] - v[i]);
  return s / dx;
}
// (w,f) = ∫ w f dx
function fF(w, P) {
  let s = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) s += P.fmid[i] * (w[i] + w[i + 1]);
  return 0.5 * s * dx;
}
// ℓ(w) = (w,f) + w(0) h
function lF(w, P) { return fF(w, P) + w[0] * P.h; }
// weak residual R(w; v) = ℓ(w) − a(w,v): the unbalanced heat that w detects
function Rw(w, v, P) { return lF(w, P) - aF(w, v, P); }
// energy Π(v) = ½ a(v,v) − ℓ(v)
function Pi(v, P) { return 0.5 * aF(v, v, P) - lF(v, P); }

function hat(XA, he) { return xs.map(x => Math.max(0, 1 - Math.abs(x - XA) / he)); }

function pts(arr, s, step = 10) {
  const out = [];
  for (let i = 0; i <= N; i += step) out.push({x: xs[i], y: arr[i], s});
  return out;
}

function solveDense(A0, b0) {
  const n = b0.length, A = A0.map(r => r.slice()), b = b0.slice();
  for (let k = 0; k < n; k++) {
    let p = k;
    for (let i = k + 1; i < n; i++) if (Math.abs(A[i][k]) > Math.abs(A[p][k])) p = i;
    [A[k], A[p]] = [A[p], A[k]]; [b[k], b[p]] = [b[p], b[k]];
    for (let i = k + 1; i < n; i++) {
      const m = A[i][k] / A[k][k];
      for (let j = k; j < n; j++) A[i][j] -= m * A[k][j];
      b[i] -= m * b[k];
    }
  }
  const x = new Array(n).fill(0);
  for (let i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
    let s = b[i];
    for (let j = i + 1; j < n; j++) s -= A[i][j] * x[j];
    x[i] = s / A[i][i];
  }
  return x;
}

// Galerkin with n linear elements: test with each hat N_A (A = 0, ..., n-1); d_n = g
function galerkin(n, P) {
  const he = 1 / n;
  const X = Array.from({length: n + 1}, (_, A) => A * he);
  const H = X.map(XA => hat(XA, he));
  const K = Array.from({length: n + 1}, () => new Array(n + 1).fill(0));
  for (let A = 0; A <= n; A++)
    for (let B = Math.max(0, A - 1); B <= Math.min(n, A + 1); B++) K[A][B] = aF(H[A], H[B], P);
  const F = H.map(w => lF(w, P));
  const Kff = K.slice(0, n).map(r => r.slice(0, n));
  const rhs = F.slice(0, n).map((FA, A) => FA - K[A][n] * P.g);
  const d = [...solveDense(Kff, rhs), P.g];
  const uh = xs.map((_, i) => d.reduce((s, dA, A) => s + dA * H[A][i], 0));
  return {n, X, H, K, F, d, uh};
}

fmt = (v, k = 3) => (Math.abs(v) < 5e-4 ? 0 : v).toFixed(k)
colors = ({exact: "#9a9a9a", u: "#1a1a1a", q: "#0d9488", cand: "#1f6feb", gal: "#c0392b",
           test: "#0d9488", cv: "#e67e22", bdry: "#4a7ba7"})
```

## Poisson's equation is a conservation law {#sec-wf-conservation}

Take any control volume $B$ inside the body. At steady state its temperature does not
change, so the heat leaving it must equal the heat generated inside it:

::: {.derivation}
$$
\underbrace{\int_{\partial B}\underline q\cdot\underline n\,d\Gamma}_{\text{net heat leaving }B}
=
\underbrace{\int_B f\,d\Omega}_{\text{heat generated inside }B}
\qquad\text{for every } B.
$$
:::

This is conservation of energy. Applying the divergence theorem and then shrinking $B$
around an arbitrary point gives the local balance $\nabla\cdot\underline q=f$. Fourier's
law supplies the material response, $\underline q=-\underline{\underline K}\nabla u$:
heat flows down the temperature gradient. Put the two physical statements together:

::: {.derivation}
$$
\boxed{-\nabla\cdot\left(\underline{\underline K}\nabla u\right)=f}
\qquad\text{in }\Omega.
$$
:::

That is Poisson's equation. It is not fundamentally a statement about curvature: it is
**local energy bookkeeping plus a flux law**.

In the wall, a control volume is an interval $[a, b]$ and its boundary is the two end
points, so the balance reads

::: {.derivation}
$$
\underbrace{q(b)}_{\text{out at } b} \;-\; \underbrace{q(a)}_{\text{in at } a}
\;=\; \underbrace{\int_a^b f\,dx}_{\text{generated inside}}
\qquad\text{for every } a<b.
$$ {#eq-wf-cv}
:::

Divide by $b - a$ and let $b \to a$: $q_{,x} = f$, and with Fourier's law,
$-\left(\kappa u_{,x}\right)_{,x} = f$.

::: {.step}
**The Poisson equation is conservation of energy on infinitely small control volumes,
applied at every point.** Hold on to that sentence. The weak form turns out to be the
same conservation law applied to finite, soft-edged control volumes.
:::

Drag the control volume below. Whatever the setup, *heat out − heat in = heat
generated*. Notice also that with $\kappa_1\neq\kappa_2$ the temperature has a **kink** at
$x=0.5$ while the flux $q$ stays continuous: energy cannot pile up at the interface. At
the kink $u_{,xx}$ does not exist, so the strong form cannot even be evaluated there.
That matters in @sec-wf-test.

## Classroom prompts
- Set $h=0$ and the source to "none". Why is $u$ constant? (Nothing is heating the wall.)
- Make $\kappa_2$ small, like an insulating layer. Why does the temperature *slope* get
  steeper on the right while $q$ does not change at all?
- Pull $a$ all the way to $0$. The heat entering is now $h$: the boundary condition is
  just the energy balance of a control volume that touches the wall's face.
:::

## Why multiply by a test function and integrate? {#sec-wf-test}

### Checking that something is zero by taking measurements

For a candidate temperature $v$, the **strong residual** is its local imbalance:

::: {.derivation}
$$
r(v) = f + \left(\kappa\,v_{,x}\right)_{,x}
\qquad\left(\text{in general, } r(v) = f + \nabla\cdot\left(\underline{\underline K}\nabla v\right)\right).
$$
:::

The strong form demands $r(u) = 0$ at every point. How else could you check that
something is zero? For a vector $\mathbf r\in\mathbb R^3$, you can dot it against every
basis vector, $\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf e_1=\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf e_2=\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf
e_3=0$, or equivalently require $\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf w=0$ for **every** vector
$\mathbf w$. A function $r(x)$ is a vector with one "component" for each point $x$, and
the dot product $\sum_i w_i r_i$ becomes $\int w\,r\,dx$. So

::: {.derivation}
$$
r(x) = 0 \ \text{ everywhere}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\int_\Omega w\,r\,dx = 0 \ \text{ for every } w .
$$
:::

::: {.step}
The $\Leftarrow$ direction is one line: choose $w=r$, and $\int r^2\,dx=0$ forces
$r\equiv 0$. (Our test functions must vanish on $\Gamma_g$, so the proof in
[Class 5](5_Class.qmd) uses $w = r\,\phi$ with $\phi > 0$ inside $\Omega$ and $\phi = 0$
on its boundary. The idea is the same.)
:::

Think of $w$ as a **sensor**. A real thermocouple never measures at a mathematical
point: it reports a weighted average over its footprint, and $w(x)$ is that footprint's
sensitivity. A broad $w$ checks a global average, a narrow bump checks a neighbourhood,
and a sign-changing $w$ compares one region with another. One sensor is not enough,
because positive and negative residuals can cancel under it. But if **every** admissible
sensor reads zero, no hidden imbalance can remain.

::: {.step}
**Strong** means the equation holds pointwise. **Weak** means every possible sensor
reads zero.
:::

### Move one derivative, and the boundary appears

Weighting the residual of the true solution still involves second derivatives of $u$.
Integration by parts moves one derivative from $u$ to $w$:

::: {.derivation}
$$
\begin{aligned}
0 &= \int_0^1 w\left[f + \left(\kappa u_{,x}\right)_{,x}\right] dx \\
&= \int_0^1 w\,f\,dx - \int_0^1 w_{,x}\,\kappa\,u_{,x}\,dx
+ \underbrace{w(1)}_{=\,0}\,\kappa u_{,x}(1) + w(0)\,\underbrace{\left(-\kappa u_{,x}(0)\right)}_{=\,h}.
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

The test function vanishes at the thermostat, and the flux condition supplies the other
end, which leaves the weak form of @sec-wf-model. In several dimensions, integration by
parts is the divergence theorem, and the same steps read

::: {.derivation}
$$
\begin{aligned}
0&=\int_\Omega w\left[f+\nabla\cdot(\underline{\underline K}\nabla u)\right]d\Omega \\
&=\int_\Omega wf\,d\Omega
-\int_\Omega \nabla w\cdot\underline{\underline K}\nabla u\,d\Omega
+\int_\Gamma w\left(\underline{\underline K}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline n\,d\Gamma,
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

and because $w=0$ on $\Gamma_g$ and
$(\underline{\underline K}\nabla u)\cdot\underline n=h$ on $\Gamma_h$,

::: {.derivation}
$$
\boxed{
a(w,u):=\int_\Omega \nabla w\cdot\underline{\underline K}\nabla u\,d\Omega
=
\underbrace{\int_\Omega wf\,d\Omega+\int_{\Gamma_h}wh\,d\Gamma}_{\ell(w)}
\quad\forall w\in\mathcal V.}
$$
:::

### A test function is a soft control volume

Now the physics. Take $w$ to be a trapezoid: $w = 1$ on $[a, b]$, dropping to $0$ over a
thin ramp of width $\delta$ on each side. Its slope $w_{,x}$ is $+1/\delta$ on the left
ramp, $-1/\delta$ on the right ramp, and zero elsewhere. With $q = -\kappa u_{,x}$,

::: {.derivation}
$$
\begin{aligned}
a(w,u) &= \int_0^1 w_{,x}\,\kappa u_{,x}\,dx = -\int_0^1 w_{,x}\, q\,dx \\
&= \underbrace{\overline{q}\big|_{\text{right ramp}}}_{\text{heat out at } b}
\;-\; \underbrace{\overline{q}\big|_{\text{left ramp}}}_{\text{heat in at } a}
\;\xrightarrow{\ \delta\to 0\ }\; q(b)-q(a),
\end{aligned}
$$
$$
(w,f) = \int_0^1 w f\,dx \;\xrightarrow{\ \delta\to 0\ }\; \int_a^b f\,dx ,
$$
:::

where $\overline q$ is the average of $q$ over a ramp.

```{python fig_softcv}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

a_, b_, dl = 0.30, 0.60, 0.06
x = np.linspace(0, 1, 4001)
w = np.clip(np.minimum((x - (a_ - dl)) / dl, ((b_ + dl) - x) / dl), 0, 1)
left = (x >= a_ - dl) & (x <= a_)
right = (x >= b_) & (x <= b_ + dl)
q = q_exact(x)
qL, qR = q[left].mean(), q[right].mean()
area = np.trapezoid(w, x)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(8.6, 6.9), sharex=True,
                         gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=[1.0, 0.9, 1.3]))
for axx in axes:
    for lo, hi in ((a_ - dl, a_), (b_, b_ + dl)):
        axx.axvspan(lo, hi, color="0.88", lw=0, zorder=0)

ax = axes[0]
ax.fill_between(x, 0, w, color=HOTCLR, alpha=0.18, lw=0, zorder=1)
ax.plot(x, w, color=HOTCLR, lw=2.4, zorder=2)
ax.text((a_ + b_) / 2, 1.1, "$w = 1$ on $[a, b]$: the control volume",
        ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=10.5, color="#a0520d")
for xv, lab in ((a_, "$a$"), (b_, "$b$")):
    ax.plot([xv, xv], [0, 1], color=DIMCLR, lw=0.8, ls=":")
    ax.text(xv, -0.1, lab, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=11)
ax.set_ylim(-0.3, 1.45)
ax.set_yticks([0, 1])
graph(ax, None, "$w$")

ax = axes[1]
wx = np.where(left, 1 / dl, 0.0) + np.where(right, -1 / dl, 0.0)
ax.fill_between(x, 0, wx, color=INK, alpha=0.12, lw=0)
ax.plot(x, wx, color=INK, lw=1.8)
ax.axhline(0, color=DIMCLR, lw=0.8)
ax.text(a_ - dl - 0.01, 0.75 / dl, r"$+1/\delta$ on the left ramp", ha="right",
        va="center", fontsize=10.5)
ax.text(b_ + dl + 0.01, -0.75 / dl, r"$-1/\delta$ on the right ramp",
        ha="left", va="center", fontsize=10.5)
ax.set_ylim(-1.4 / dl, 1.4 / dl)
ax.set_yticks([])
graph(ax, None, r"$w_{,x}$")

ax = axes[2]
ax.plot(x, q, color=FLUXCLR, lw=2.4)
ax.plot([a_ - dl / 2], [qL], "o", color=FLUXCLR, ms=7, zorder=5)
ax.plot([b_ + dl / 2], [qR], "o", color=FLUXCLR, ms=7, zorder=5)
ax.annotate(r"$\overline{q}$ on the left ramp = %.2f: heat in" % qL,
            xy=(a_ - dl / 2, qL), xytext=(0.02, qL + 0.62), fontsize=10.5,
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=INK, lw=0.8))
ax.annotate(r"$\overline{q}$ on the right ramp = %.2f: heat out" % qR,
            xy=(b_ + dl / 2, qR), xytext=(0.63, qR - 0.95), fontsize=10.5,
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=INK, lw=0.8))
ax.set_ylim(0, 2.9)
graph(ax, "$x$", r"heat flux $q = -\kappa u_{,x}$")
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.6)
fig_softcv_path = save(fig, "WF_Fig2_SoftControlVolume.png")
SOFTCV = dict(qL=qL, qR=qR, area=area, a=a_, b=b_, dl=dl)
```

![A test function as a soft control volume, drawn for the default setup. Top: the
trapezoid $w$. Middle: its slope, non-zero only on the two ramps (shaded), which act as
the control volume's walls. Bottom: the heat flux of the exact solution. $a(w, u)$
subtracts the average flux over the left ramp from the average over the right ramp: heat
out minus heat in.](`{python} fig_softcv_path`){#fig-wf-softcv width=80%}

```{python softcv_numbers}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

print(r"""
::: {.step}
For the default setup in @fig-wf-softcv, $a(w, u) = %.2f - %.2f = %.2f$, and the heat
generated inside the soft control volume is $(w, f) = f \int w\,dx = 2 \times %.2f =
%.2f$. The two agree, as the weak form says they must.
:::
""" % (SOFTCV["qR"], SOFTCV["qL"], SOFTCV["qR"] - SOFTCV["qL"], SOFTCV["area"],
       FTOT * SOFTCV["area"]))
```

So $a(w,u) = (w,f)$ **is exactly the control-volume balance @eq-wf-cv**. The slope of
the test function marks the walls of the control volume, and $a(w,u)$ adds up the heat
crossing those walls. If the control volume reaches the left face ($w(0)=1$), the heat
$h$ entering there is counted too, which is the $w(0)\,h$ term. A general $w$ is just a
*softer* control volume, a weighted region:

::: {.step}
**Energy is balanced on every soft control volume you can draw.** The strong form says it
is balanced on every infinitesimal one. Same physics, different bookkeeping.
:::

### Why this bookkeeping is better

1. **A pointwise balance becomes a family of weighted balances**, one for each soft
   control volume. Finitely many of them give finitely many equations, which is
   Galerkin's method (@sec-wf-galerkin).
2. **Only one derivative lands on $u$.** The composite wall has a physical kink at
   $x=0.5$, where $u_{,xx}$ does not exist. The weak form does not care, and neither do
   the kinked hat functions of finite elements.
3. **The flux condition enters on its own**, as the heat crossing the wall of a control
   volume that touches $\Gamma_h$. Trial functions never have to satisfy it, which is why
   it is called *natural*.
4. **Test functions vanish on $\Gamma_g$ for a physical reason.** The thermostat supplies
   whatever heat flux is needed to hold $u = g$, and that flux is unknown in advance: it
   is a reaction. We cannot write a balance for a control volume that includes that
   face, so we do not. The reaction can still be recovered afterwards.
   (@sec-wf-energy gives the energy reason.)

### Interactive: probe a candidate with test functions {#sec-wf-probe}

Choose a candidate temperature $v$ and a test function $w$. The readout gives the
**weak residual** $R(w; v) = (w,f)+w(0)h-a(w,v)$: the *unbalanced heat* inside the soft
control volume $w$. The bottom plot sweeps a whole **family** of tests. Things to notice:

- **Exact solution:** every probe reads zero.
- **Straight-line guess** or **exact + wiggle:** most probes read non-zero.
- **Galerkin $u^h$:** the finite-element hats $N_A$ read *exactly* zero, but bumps and
  cosines generally do **not**. Galerkin only guarantees the tests it was asked to pass.
  (A curiosity of 1D linear elements: when a node sits on the material interface, which
  happens when $n$ is even, $u^h$ is exact *at the nodes*, yet it still fails other
  probes.)

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof cand2 = Inputs.radio(["exact solution u", "Galerkin solution uʰ", "straight-line guess", "exact + wiggle"],
  {value: "straight-line guess", label: "candidate v"})
viewof n2 = Inputs.range([1, 12], {value: 4, step: 1, label: "elements n (for uʰ and hats)"})
viewof test2 = Inputs.radio(["soft control volume", "bump", "FE hat N_A", "cosine mode"],
  {value: "soft control volume", label: "test function w"})
viewof c2 = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.3, step: 0.01, label: "center (CV / bump / hat)"})
viewof s2 = Inputs.range([0.02, 0.5], {value: 0.1, step: 0.01, label: "half-width (CV / bump)"})
viewof m2 = Inputs.range([1, 8], {value: 2, step: 1, label: "mode m (cosine)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
G2 = galerkin(n2, P)
cands = {
  const u = P.u, g = P.g, u0 = u[0];
  const amp = 0.15 * (Math.max(...u) - Math.min(...u) + 0.5);
  return {
    "exact solution u": u,
    "Galerkin solution uʰ": G2.uh,
    "straight-line guess": xs.map(x => u0 + (g - u0) * x),
    "exact + wiggle": u.map((ui, i) => ui + amp * Math.sin(3 * Math.PI * xs[i]))
  };
}
v2 = cands[cand2]

function testFn(type, c, s, m, n) {
  const del = 0.02;
  if (type === "soft control volume") {
    const b = Math.min(c + s, 1 - del), a = Math.min(c - s, b);
    return xs.map(x => x < a ? Math.max(0, 1 - (a - x) / del) : x <= b ? 1 : Math.max(0, 1 - (x - b) / del));
  }
  if (type === "bump") {
    const cc = Math.min(c, 1 - s);
    return xs.map(x => Math.max(0, 1 - Math.abs(x - cc) / s));
  }
  if (type === "FE hat N_A") {
    const A = Math.min(n - 1, Math.round(c * n));
    return hat(A / n, 1 / n);
  }
  return xs.map(x => Math.cos((m - 0.5) * Math.PI * x));
}

w2 = testFn(test2, c2, s2, m2, n2)
probe = {
  const gen = fF(w2, P), wall = w2[0] * P.h, out = aF(w2, v2, P);
  return {gen, wall, out, R: gen + wall - out};
}
family2 = {
  if (test2 === "FE hat N_A")
    return d3.range(n2).map(A => ({p: A / n2, R: Rw(hat(A / n2, 1 / n2), v2, P)}));
  if (test2 === "cosine mode")
    return d3.range(1, 9).map(m => ({p: m, R: Rw(testFn(test2, 0, 0, m, n2), v2, P)}));
  return d3.range(0, 1.0001, 0.02).map(c => ({p: c, R: Rw(testFn(test2, c, s2, m2, n2), v2, P)}));
}
pCur = test2 === "FE hat N_A" ? Math.min(n2 - 1, Math.round(c2 * n2)) / n2
     : test2 === "cosine mode" ? m2 : c2
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const W = Math.min(width, 780);
  const marks = [
    Plot.line(pts(P.u, "exact u"), {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: colors.exact, strokeWidth: 6, strokeOpacity: 0.45}),
    Plot.line(pts(v2, "candidate v"), {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: cand2.startsWith("Galerkin") ? colors.gal : colors.cand, strokeWidth: 2})
  ];
  if (cand2.startsWith("Galerkin")) marks.push(Plot.dot(G2.X.map((x, A) => ({x, y: G2.d[A]})), {x: "x", y: "y", fill: colors.gal, r: 4}));
  const top = Plot.plot({height: 200, width: W, marginLeft: 50, grid: true, x: {domain: [0, 1], label: "x"},
    y: {label: "v(x)  (grey = exact u)"}, marks});

    y: {label: "test w(x)"},

            Plot.line(pts(w2, "w", 5), {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: colors.test, strokeWidth: 2}), Plot.ruleY([0])]});
  const xlab = test2 === "cosine mode" ? "mode m" : test2 === "FE hat N_A" ? "node location x_A" : "test-function center";
  const bot = Plot.plot({height: 170, width: W, marginLeft: 50, grid: true,
    x: {label: xlab}, y: {label: "R(w; v) for the family"},
    marks: [Plot.ruleY([0]),
            Plot.line(family2, {x: "p", y: "R", stroke: colors.test, strokeOpacity: 0.6}),
            Plot.dot(family2, {x: "p", y: "R", fill: colors.test, r: 3}),
            Plot.dot([{p: pCur, R: probe.R}], {x: "p", y: "R", r: 7, stroke: "black", strokeWidth: 2})]});
  return html`<div>${top}${mid}${bot}</div>`;
}
```

```{ojs}
<tr><td>heat entering through the left face, &nbsp;w(0) h</td><td style="text-align:right">${fmt(probe.wall)}</td></tr>

<tr><td><b>unbalanced heat, &nbsp;R(w; v) = (w,f) + w(0)h − a(w,v)</b></td><td style="text-align:right"><b>${fmt(probe.R)}</b></td></tr>
```

## Trial functions and test functions {#sec-wf-spaces}

The two spaces answer two different questions:

::: {.derivation}
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal S
&=\{v\in H^1(\Omega):v=g\text{ on }\Gamma_g\}
&&\text{Which fields may be the answer?}\\
\mathcal V
&=\{w\in H^1(\Omega):w=0\text{ on }\Gamma_g\}
&&\text{Which probes may we use?}
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

::: {.step .notes}
- A **trial function** $v\in\mathcal S$ is a candidate answer. It already obeys every
  essential (Dirichlet) boundary condition, but it need not obey the differential
  equation.
- A **test function** $w\in\mathcal V$ is a probe and an allowable perturbation. It is
  zero where the value of the answer is fixed.
- If $v_1,v_2\in\mathcal S$, then $v_1-v_2\in\mathcal V$. So $\mathcal S$ is a shifted,
  or affine, copy of $\mathcal V$: $\mathcal S = g + \mathcal V$, with the same shapes
  lifted to the Dirichlet value. That is why the Galerkin form writes $u^h = v^h + g^h$
  with $v^h \in \mathcal V^h$.
- If $u\in\mathcal S$ and $w\in\mathcal V$, then $u+\epsilon w\in\mathcal S$ for every
  $\epsilon$. A test function is literally a direction in which an admissible trial field
  can be varied.
:::

```{python fig_spaces}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11.8, 3.55))
x = np.linspace(0, 1, 300)
g = 0.30

ax = axes[0]
for k, v in enumerate([g + 0.8 * (1 - x), g + 0.55 * (1 - x) ** 2,
                       g + 0.35 * np.sin(np.pi * x) * (1 - x),
                       g + 0.7 * (1 - x) - 0.35 * x * (1 - x)]):
    ax.plot(x, v, color=BASISCLRS[k], lw=1.8)
ax.plot([1], [g], "o", color=BDRYCLR, ms=7)
ax.text(0.97, g + 0.055, "$v(1)=g$", ha="right", va="bottom", color=BDRYCLR)
graph(ax, "$x$", "$v(x)$")
ax.set_title(r"trials $v\in\mathcal{S}$", fontsize=11.5)

ax = axes[1]
for k, w in enumerate([(1 - x), x * (1 - x), np.sin(np.pi * x),
                       0.65 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * x)]):
    ax.plot(x, w, color=BASISCLRS[k], lw=1.8)
ax.axhline(0, color=DIMCLR, lw=0.7)
ax.plot([1], [0], "o", color=BDRYCLR, ms=7)
ax.text(0.97, 0.09, "$w(1)=0$", ha="right", va="bottom", color=BDRYCLR)
graph(ax, "$x$", "$w(x)$")
ax.set_title(r"tests $w\in\mathcal{V}$", fontsize=11.5)

ax = axes[2]
u0 = g + 0.62 * (1 - x) + 0.10 * x * (1 - x)
w = 0.40 * np.sin(np.pi * x)
for eps, c in [(-0.65, BASISCLRS[0]), (0, INK), (0.65, BASISCLRS[1])]:
    ax.plot(x, u0 + eps * w, color=c, lw=2.2 if eps == 0 else 1.6,
            ls="-" if eps == 0 else "--")
ax.plot([1], [g], "o", color=BDRYCLR, ms=7)
ax.annotate(r"$+\,\epsilon w$", xy=(0.47, u0[140] + 0.65 * w[140]),
            xytext=(0.08, 0.66), color=FLUXCLR,
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=FLUXCLR))
graph(ax, "$x$", None)
ax.set_title(r"$u+\epsilon w$ stays admissible", fontsize=11.5)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=2.0)
fig_spaces_path = save(fig, "WF_Fig3_TrialTest.png")
```

![Trial functions are possible answers; test functions are probes and allowable
directions. Their different boundary values are not arbitrary bookkeeping: they ensure
that varying a trial field never violates its prescribed temperature.](`{python} fig_spaces_path`){#fig-wf-trial-test width=100%}

| | **Trial function** | **Test function** |
|---|---|---|
| Symbol and space | $u, v\in\mathcal S$ (discrete: $u^h\in\mathcal S^h$) | $w\in\mathcal V$ (discrete: $w^h\in\mathcal V^h$) |
| Job | a **candidate answer**: a temperature field we try out | a **probe** that tests the candidate: a sensor, a soft control volume, a nudge direction |
| On $\Gamma_g$ (essential condition) | must equal $g$: the thermostat is non-negotiable | must be $0$: we cannot nudge there, and its flux is an unknown reaction |
| On $\Gamma_h$ (natural condition) | nothing imposed | nothing imposed; the flux $h$ is enforced *by the tests*, through $w(0)\,h$ |
| Energy picture (@sec-wf-energy) | a point on the energy landscape | a direction in which you may step |
| In finite element code | $u^h = \sum_A d_A N_A + g^h$, with unknowns $d_A$ | $w^h = N_A$: **one equation per test function** |

## The weak solution minimizes an energy {#sec-wf-energy}

### One spring first

For a single spring of stiffness $k$ under a load $F$, the total potential energy is
$\Pi(d)=\tfrac12 k d^2 - F d$. At the minimum the slope is zero: $\Pi'(d) = kd-F=0$.
Now "nudge" the displacement by $\epsilon w$:

::: {.derivation}
$$
\Pi(d+\epsilon w) = \Pi(d) + \epsilon\,w\,(k d - F) + \tfrac12\epsilon^2 k w^2 .
$$
:::

::: {.step}
$d$ is the minimizer exactly when the term linear in $\epsilon$ vanishes for every nudge
$w$: $\;w\,k\,d = w\,F$ for all $w$. That is the weak form of $kd = F$.
:::

### The same thing for the wall

Replace numbers by functions: $w\,k\,d$ becomes $a(w,u)$ and $wF$ becomes $\ell(w)$.
Assume $\underline{\underline K}$ is symmetric and positive definite (here, $\kappa > 0$)
and that $\Gamma_g$ is not empty, so the solution is unique. For every trial function
$v\in\mathcal S$, define the energy

::: {.derivation}
$$
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\Pi(v) &= \underbrace{\frac12\,a(v,v)}_{\text{cost of gradients}}
- \underbrace{\ell(v)}_{\text{payoff from heat supplied}} \\
&= \frac12\int_\Omega \nabla v\cdot\underline{\underline K}\nabla v\,d\Omega
-\int_\Omega v\,f\,d\Omega-\int_{\Gamma_h}v\,h\,d\Gamma
\end{aligned}}
$$
:::

The first term penalizes gradients; the source and boundary terms tilt that bowl. Nudge
the solution in a direction $w\in\mathcal V$:

::: {.derivation}
$$
\Pi(u+\epsilon w) \;=\; \Pi(u) \;+\; \epsilon\,\underbrace{\big[a(w,u) - \ell(w)\big]}_{-R(w;\,u)} \;+\; \tfrac12\epsilon^2\,\underbrace{a(w,w)}_{\ge\, 0} .
$$
:::

As a function of $\epsilon$ this is a **parabola** that opens upward, because
$a(w,w) = \int \kappa\,(w_{,x})^2\,dx \ge 0$: this is where the symmetry and positivity
of $a(\cdot,\cdot)$ pay off. $u$ is the lowest point exactly when the parabola is flat at
$\epsilon=0$ for **every** allowed direction $w$:

::: {.derivation}
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{d}{d\epsilon}\Pi(u+\epsilon w)\Big|_{\epsilon=0}=0\quad\forall w\in\mathcal V \\
\Longleftrightarrow\quad
&\boxed{\;a(w,u)=\ell(w)\quad\forall w\in\mathcal V\;}
\qquad\text{which is } (\mathrm{W}).
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

And it is a minimum, not merely a flat spot. For any $v\in\mathcal S$, let
$e=v-u\in\mathcal V$. Expanding $\Pi(u + e)$ and using the weak form with $w=e$,

::: {.derivation}
$$
\Pi(v)-\Pi(u)=\frac12\,a(e,e)\ \ge\ 0 ,
$$
:::

with equality only when $e = 0$.

::: {.step}
So a **test function is a direction in which you may nudge the temperature field**, and
the weak form says that *no allowed nudge lowers the energy*. **Allowed** means that the
nudged field must still be a trial function: $u+\epsilon w = g$ at $x=1$, so $w(1)=0$.
That is the energy reason why $\mathcal V$ has homogeneous essential conditions.
:::

### Interactive: nudge a candidate and watch the energy

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof cand3 = Inputs.radio(["exact solution u", "straight-line guess", "Galerkin uʰ (2 elements)"],
  {value: "exact solution u", label: "start from v ="})
viewof dir3 = Inputs.radio(["1 − x", "cos(πx/2)", "cos(3πx/2)", "bump at x = 0.3", "constant 1  ⚠ moves x = 1"],
  {value: "cos(πx/2)", label: "nudge direction w"})
viewof eps3 = Inputs.range([-1, 1], {value: 0, step: 0.01, label: "nudge size ε"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
nudge = {
  const u = P.u, u0 = u[0];
  const v = cand3 === "exact solution u" ? u
          : cand3 === "straight-line guess" ? xs.map(x => u0 + (P.g - u0) * x)
          : galerkin(2, P).uh;
  const A = 0.5 * (Math.max(...u) - Math.min(...u) + 0.4);
  const shapes = {
    "1 − x": x => 1 - x,
    "cos(πx/2)": x => Math.cos(Math.PI * x / 2),
    "cos(3πx/2)": x => Math.cos(3 * Math.PI * x / 2),
    "bump at x = 0.3": x => Math.max(0, 1 - Math.abs(x - 0.3) / 0.15),
    "constant 1  ⚠ moves x = 1": x => 1
  };
  const w = xs.map(x => A * shapes[dir3](x));
  const p0 = Pi(v, P), p1 = aF(w, v, P) - lF(w, P), p2 = aF(w, w, P);
  const curve = d3.range(-1, 1.0001, 0.02).map(e => ({e, Pi: p0 + p1 * e + 0.5 * p2 * e * e}));
  const tangent = [-1, 1].map(e => ({e, Pi: p0 + p1 * e}));
  return {v, w, p0, p1, p2, curve, tangent, PiU: Pi(u, P), cur: p0 + p1 * eps3 + 0.5 * p2 * eps3 * eps3};
}
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Classroom prompts
- Start from the **exact solution**. Every allowed direction gives a parabola with its
  bottom at $\epsilon=0$ (slope 0).
- Start from the **straight-line guess**. The parabola's bottom moves off $\epsilon=0$:
  some nudge *lowers* the energy, so the guess is not the solution. The slope is minus
  the residual from @sec-wf-probe.
- Choose **"constant 1"** while starting from the exact solution. The slope is **not**
  zero, because this nudge moves the temperature at $x=1$ off $g$. The thermostat forbids
  that direction, so it is excluded from $\mathcal V$.
:::

### Is it really an energy?

Chop the wall into slices of thickness $h_e$. Each slice conducts heat like a resistor:
the heat flowing from node $A$ to node $A+1$ is a **conductance** $\kappa/h_e$ times a
**temperature drop**, $q = \frac{\kappa}{h_e}(u_A-u_{A+1})$. That is Ohm's law, $I=V/R$,
with temperature in place of voltage. Then

::: {.derivation}
$$
\begin{aligned}
a(u,u) &= \int_0^1 \kappa\,(u_{,x})^2\,dx
\;\approx\; \sum_{\text{slices}} \frac{\kappa}{h_e}\,(u_{A+1}-u_A)^2 \\
&= \sum_{\text{slices}} \underbrace{q}_{\text{flow}}\times\underbrace{(u_A-u_{A+1})}_{\text{drop}} ,
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

and the $\approx$ is exact for a piecewise-linear $u$. In an electric circuit, "flow ×
drop" is exactly the **power dissipated**, $I\cdot V = V^2/R$. The same Poisson equation
turns up in many settings, and in most of them $\tfrac12 a(u,u)$ is a genuine energy or
power:

| Physical setting | $u$ | $\kappa$ | $\tfrac12\,a(u,u)$ is |
|---|---|---|---|
| Axially loaded rod ([1D Poisson IV](Poisson1D_Rod_FEM.qmd)) | displacement | $EA$ | the strain energy stored in the rod |
| Electrical conduction | voltage | electrical conductivity | half the Joule heating power |
| Taut membrane or soap film | deflection | tension | the stretching energy |
| **Heat conduction** | temperature | thermal conductivity | *not* a stored energy: a measure of how hard the wall works to push heat through its resistance |

::: {.callout-important title="What is, and is not, an energy"}
- $\tfrac12 a(u,u)$ is the quadratic, or **Dirichlet energy**, term.
- $a(w,u)$ with $w\ne u$ is *not* itself an energy. It multiplies the flows of state
  $u$ by the temperature drops of state $w$: it is the rate at which the energy changes
  when $u$ is nudged in the direction $w$. For a hat function, $a(N_A, u)$ is simply the
  **net heat conducted away from node $A$**.
- For steady heat conduction, $\Pi$ is a **mathematical energy functional**, not the
  body's stored thermodynamic heat. Conservation of physical energy produced the
  differential equation; minimizing $\Pi$ is an equivalent mathematical characterization
  of its solution.
- In linear elasticity the same pattern becomes literal total potential energy, and
  $a(w,u)=\ell(w)$ becomes the principle of virtual work. The algebra is shared even
  though the physical interpretation depends on the problem.
:::

## Galerkin's method: a finite menu and a finite exam {#sec-wf-galerkin}

The weak problem asks you to search an **infinite menu** of candidates ($\mathcal S$) and
pass an **infinite exam** of tests ($\mathcal V$). Galerkin's method shrinks both, and it
uses the same functions for each.

1. **Shrink the menu.** Cut the wall into $n$ elements with nodes $x_0 = 0, \dots, x_n
   = 1$, and consider only the piecewise-linear candidates
   $u^h = \sum_{B=0}^{n-1} d_B N_B + g\,N_n$. They are set by finitely many nodal values
   $d_B$, and the last term carries the thermostat value. This is
   $\mathcal S^h\subset\mathcal S$.
2. **Shrink the exam, with the same functions.** Test only with
   $w^h = \sum_{A=0}^{n-1} c_A N_A$: every hat except the one on $\Gamma_g$. This is
   $\mathcal V^h\subset\mathcal V$.
3. **Read off the equations.** Because the weak form is linear in $w$,

::: {.derivation}
$$
\sum_{A=0}^{n-1}c_A\left[a(N_A,u^h)-\ell(N_A)\right]=0
\qquad\text{for every choice of } (c_0,\ldots,c_{n-1}),
$$
:::

::: {.step}
so every bracket must vanish on its own. That gives one equation per test function:
:::

::: {.derivation}
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\sum_{B=0}^{n-1} \underbrace{a(N_A,N_B)}_{K_{AB}}\,d_B
= \underbrace{\ell(N_A) - a(N_A,N_n)\,g}_{F_A} \\
&\text{for } A = 0, \dots, n-1:\quad \text{that is,}\quad \mathbf K\mathbf d = \mathbf F .
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

::: {.step}
Each equation is **the heat balance of the soft control volume $N_A$** around node $A$.
In energy language, each equation says that **the energy landscape is flat in the $d_A$
direction**, because $\partial\Pi(u^h)/\partial d_A = a(N_A, u^h) - \ell(N_A) =
-R(N_A;\,u^h)$. For linear elements the whole system is literally a chain of thermal
resistors (@fig-wf-resistors), and $\mathbf K$ is its conductance matrix.
:::

```{python fig_resistors}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.6, 2.9))
xn = np.arange(5) * 1.6
labels = ["$d_0$", "$d_1$", "$d_2$", "$d_3$", "$g$"]


def zigzag(x0, x1, y, amp=0.12, nz=6):
    L = x1 - x0
    t = np.linspace(x0 + 0.2 * L, x1 - 0.2 * L, 2 * nz + 1)
    xz = [x0] + list(t) + [x1]
    yz = [y, y] + [y + amp * (1 if k % 2 == 0 else -1) for k in range(len(t) - 2)] \
        + [y, y]
    ax.plot(xz, yz, color=INK, lw=1.6, zorder=1)


for i in range(4):
    zigzag(xn[i] + 0.22, xn[i + 1] - 0.22, 0.0)
    ax.text((xn[i] + xn[i + 1]) / 2, 0.24, r"$\kappa/h_e$", ha="center",
            va="bottom", fontsize=11)
for i, (xv, lab) in enumerate(zip(xn, labels)):
    ax.add_patch(Circle((xv, 0), 0.22, facecolor="#fde3c8" if i < 4 else "#dbe7f3",
                        edgecolor=INK if i < 4 else BDRYCLR, lw=1.4, zorder=3))
    ax.text(xv, 0, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=12, zorder=4)
arrow(ax, (-1.15, 0), (-0.24, 0), color=FLUXCLR, lw=2.6, ms=15)
ax.text(-0.7, 0.13, "$h$ in", ha="center", va="bottom", color=FLUXCLR, fontsize=11)
ax.text(xn[-1], -0.34, "thermostat", ha="center", va="top", color=BDRYCLR,
        fontsize=10.5)
ax.text(xn[2], -0.72, r"row $A$ of $\mathbf{K}\mathbf{d} = \mathbf{F}$:  "
        "heat conducted away from node $A$ = heat supplied to node $A$",
        ha="center", va="top", fontsize=11)
tidy(ax)
ax.set_xlim(-1.35, xn[-1] + 0.6)
ax.set_ylim(-1.05, 0.6)
fig_resistors_path = save(fig, "WF_Fig4_Resistors.png")
```

### Interactive: the energy bowl with two unknowns {#sec-wf-bowl}

Use two elements, with nodes at $x=0,\,0.5,\,1$. The trial functions are
$v^h = d_0N_0 + d_1N_1 + gN_2$: a menu with two parameters, so $\Pi$ is a bowl over the
$(d_0,d_1)$ plane. Move the sliders to search the menu yourself. The arrow points
**downhill**, and its components are exactly the residuals $R(N_0)$ and $R(N_1)$: the
tests you are currently failing.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
G = galerkin(2, P)
rng5 = {
  const d = G.d, lo = Math.min(d[0], d[1], P.g) - 1, hi = Math.max(d[0], d[1], P.g) + 1;
  return [Math.floor(lo * 10) / 10, Math.ceil(hi * 10) / 10];
}
PiD = (a, b) => {
  const D = [a, b, P.g];
  let s = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { s -= G.F[i] * D[i]; for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) s += 0.5 * D[i] * G.K[i][j] * D[j]; }
  return s;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false

viewof d1 = Inputs.range(rng5, {value: P.g, step: 0.01, label: "d₁ = vʰ(0.5)"})

  for (const [el, val] of [[viewof d0, G.d[0]], [viewof d1, G.d[1]]]) {
    el.value = val; el.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true}));
  }
}})
```

```{ojs}
    const a = lo + (i + 0.5) * st, b = lo + (j + 0.5) * st;

            Plot.line(vh, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: colors.cand, strokeWidth: 2.5}),

  return html`<div style="display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:12px;align-items:flex-start">${bowl}<div>${curve}

      <tr><td>Π(vʰ)</td><td style="text-align:right">${fmt(PiD(d0, d1))}</td></tr>

      <tr><td>Π(u), exact (not on this menu)</td><td style="text-align:right">${fmt(Pi(P.u, P))}</td></tr>
      <tr><td>R(N₀) = −∂Π/∂d₀</td><td style="text-align:right"><b>${fmt(R0)}</b></td></tr>
```

### Interactive: enlarge the menu

More elements means a bigger menu $\mathcal S^h$ and a bigger exam $\mathcal V^h$. On
nested meshes ($n = 2, 4, 8, 16$) each menu contains the previous one, so the Galerkin
energy can only go down toward $\Pi(u)$. The gap is exactly the error, measured in
energy:

::: {.derivation}
$$
a\left(u-u^h,\,u-u^h\right) \;=\; 2\,\big[\Pi(u^h)-\Pi(u)\big] \;\ge 0 .
$$
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof n6 = Inputs.range([1, 16], {value: 3, step: 1, label: "number of elements n"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
G6 = galerkin(n6, P)
PiU = Pi(P.u, P)
energies = d3.range(1, 17).map(n => ({n, Pi: Pi(galerkin(n, P).uh, P)}))
```


### Galerkin orthogonality: the best candidate on the menu

The weak form holds for every $w\in\mathcal V$, so in particular for every
$w^h\in\mathcal V^h$. Subtracting the Galerkin equations from it leaves

::: {.derivation}
$$
a\left(w^h,\; u-u^h\right) = 0 \qquad \forall\, w^h\in\mathcal V^h .
$$
:::

This is **Galerkin orthogonality**. The error is not generally zero, but no test in the
finite exam can detect it: it is invisible to every retained test when measured with
$a(\cdot,\cdot)$. Adding elements or raising the polynomial degree enlarges
$\mathcal V^h$, asks more questions, and leaves the error fewer places to hide.

Because $\Pi(v) - \Pi(u) = \tfrac12\,a(v - u,\, v - u)$ for every trial function $v$,
the lowest-energy candidate on the menu is also the one closest to $u$ in the energy
norm:

::: {.derivation}
$$
\begin{aligned}
&u^h=\underset{v^h\in\mathcal S^h}{\operatorname{argmin}}\;\Pi(v^h) \\
\Longleftrightarrow\quad
&a\left(u-u^h,\,u-u^h\right) \;\le\; a\left(u-v^h,\,u-v^h\right)
\quad\forall\, v^h\in\mathcal S^h
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

```{python fig_geometry}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.2, 5.0))
V = np.array([[0.6, 0.3], [4.8, 0.3], [5.9, 1.55], [1.7, 1.55]])
lift = np.array([0.0, 2.25])
ax.add_patch(MplPolygon(V, closed=True, facecolor=to_rgba(FLUXCLR, 0.12),
                        edgecolor=FLUXCLR, lw=1.4))
ax.add_patch(MplPolygon(V + lift, closed=True, facecolor=to_rgba(REACTCLR, 0.10),
                        edgecolor=REACTCLR, lw=1.4))
O = np.array([2.3, 0.75])
ax.plot(*O, "o", color=INK, ms=5, zorder=5)
ax.text(O[0] - 0.1, O[1] - 0.06, "0", ha="right", va="top", fontsize=11)
arrow(ax, tuple(O), tuple(O + lift - np.array([0, 0.06])), color=DIMCLR, lw=1.8,
      ms=12)
ax.text(O[0] - 0.12, O[1] + 0.5 * lift[1], "lift $g$", ha="right",
        va="center", color=DIMCLR, fontsize=11)
dvec = np.array([1.0, 0.18])
dvec = dvec / np.linalg.norm(dvec)
P1, P2 = O - 1.4 * dvec, O + 2.6 * dvec
ax.plot(*zip(P1, P2), color=FLUXCLR, lw=3, zorder=4)
ax.plot(*zip(P1 + lift, P2 + lift), color=REACTCLR, lw=3, zorder=4)
ax.text(*(P2 + np.array([0.1, -0.12])), r"$\mathcal{V}^h \subset \mathcal{V}$",
        color=FLUXCLR, va="top", fontsize=11.5)
ax.text(*(P2 + lift + np.array([0.1, -0.12])),
        r"$\mathcal{S}^h \subset \mathcal{S}$", color=REACTCLR, va="top",
        fontsize=11.5)
ax.text(6.0, 0.9, "$\\mathcal{V}$: $w = 0$ on $\\Gamma_g$", color=FLUXCLR,
        fontsize=11.5, va="center")
ax.text(6.0, 3.15, "$\\mathcal{S} = g + \\mathcal{V}$:\n$u = g$ on $\\Gamma_g$",
        color=REACTCLR, fontsize=11.5, va="center")
base = O + lift
uu = base + np.array([1.0, 0.6])
t = (uu - base) @ dvec
uh = base + t * dvec
nrm = (uu - uh) / np.linalg.norm(uu - uh)
ax.plot(*zip(uh, uu), color=LOADCLR, lw=1.8, ls="--", zorder=5)
sq = 0.12
ax.plot([uh[0] + sq * dvec[0], uh[0] + sq * dvec[0] + sq * nrm[0],
         uh[0] + sq * nrm[0]],
        [uh[1] + sq * dvec[1], uh[1] + sq * dvec[1] + sq * nrm[1],
         uh[1] + sq * nrm[1]], color=LOADCLR, lw=1.2, zorder=5)
ax.plot(*uu, "o", color=INK, ms=7, zorder=6)
ax.text(uu[0] + 0.14, uu[1], "$u$ (exact)", fontsize=11.5, va="center")
ax.plot(*uh, "o", color=LOADCLR, ms=7, zorder=6)
ax.text(uh[0] - 0.12, uh[1] - 0.1, "$u^h$", color=LOADCLR, ha="right",
        va="top", fontsize=12.5)
mid = 0.5 * (uh + uu)
ax.text(mid[0] - 0.14, mid[1] + 0.08, "$e = u - u^h$", color=LOADCLR,
        fontsize=11, ha="right", va="center")
ax.text(3.6, -0.15, "Galerkin: $u^h$ is the member of $\\mathcal{S}^h$ closest to "
        "$u$ in energy, because $a(w^h, e) = 0$ for every $w^h \\in \\mathcal{V}^h$",
        ha="center", va="top", fontsize=11)
tidy(ax)
ax.set_xlim(0.2, 8.6)
ax.set_ylim(-0.75, 4.1)
fig_geometry_path = save(fig, "WF_Fig5_Geometry.png")
```

![Function spaces as geometry. $\mathcal V$ passes through $0$; $\mathcal S$ is the same
set of shapes lifted by the Dirichlet value, so it misses $0$ and is not itself a vector
space. Galerkin chooses a finite slice of each ($\mathcal S^h$ and $\mathcal V^h$). The
exact $u$ usually lies off the slice, and $u^h$ is its foot, with the error
perpendicular to the slice when angles are measured with
$a(\cdot,\cdot)$.](`{python} fig_geometry_path`){#fig-wf-geometry width=86%}

::: {.callout-note title="Galerkin versus Petrov–Galerkin"}
"Weighted residual" only requires some finite collection of tests. **Galerkin** (also
called Bubnov–Galerkin) specifically uses the same basis functions for the trial
correction and for the tests, which is what makes $\mathbf K$ symmetric and gives the
energy and best-approximation properties above. Methods that use a different test space
are called Petrov–Galerkin methods.
:::

## Summary {#sec-wf-summary}

### The weak form, said three ways

| | Strong form (S) | Weak form (W) | Galerkin (G) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Conservation** | balance on every infinitesimal control volume | balance on every soft control volume $w$ | balance on the $n$ nodal control volumes $N_A$ |
| **Measurement** | the residual is zero at every point | every sensor $w$ reads zero | the sensors $N_A$ read zero; others might not |
| **Energy** | (hidden) | $u$ minimizes $\Pi$ over $\mathcal S$: no allowed nudge lowers it | $u^h$ minimizes $\Pi$ over the menu $\mathcal S^h$ |
| **Derivatives on $u$** | two | one | one (piecewise-linear is fine) |
| **Flux condition $h$** | imposed on $u$ | enters through the tests, as $w(0)\,h$ | row $A=0$ of $\mathbf F$ |
| **Temperature condition $g$** | imposed on $u$ | built into $\mathcal S$; $w=0$ there | $d_n=g$; no test $N_n$ |

### The vocabulary on one page

| Object | Plain-language meaning | Mathematical job |
|---|---|---|
| $u$ | the unknown physical field | the exact solution, in $\mathcal S$ |
| $v\in\mathcal S$ | a candidate answer | obeys the essential boundary data |
| $w\in\mathcal V$ | a probe, a soft control volume, an allowed direction | vanishes on $\Gamma_g$ |
| $r(v)$ | local imbalance | zero at every point in the strong form |
| $\int w\,r(v)$ | one sensor reading | zero for every $w$ in the weak form |
| $a(w,u)$ | heat crossing the walls of $w$; the rate of change of energy in direction $w$ | left side of the weak form |
| $\Pi(v)$ | an energy landscape | minimized by the weak solution |
| $\mathcal S^h,\mathcal V^h$ | finite menus of fields and probes | where approximation enters |
| $N_A$ | one nodal trial pattern and test | turns the weak form into row $A$ of $\mathbf K\mathbf d = \mathbf F$ |

::: {.callout-tip title="A five-minute explanation to remember"}
1. **Conservation** says that the flux leaving any small region equals what is generated
   inside it.
2. The **strong form** insists on that balance point by point.
3. A **test function** is an adjustable probe, a soft control volume. Zero response to
   every probe is another way to say that there is no imbalance anywhere.
4. **Integration by parts** makes the probing practical: it lowers the derivative order
   and exposes the boundary fluxes.
5. **Trial functions** are allowed answers; test functions are allowed questions and
   directions.
6. The weak solution is the bottom of an **energy** bowl.
7. **Galerkin** searches a finite slice of that bowl and asks only a finite basis of
   questions. That restriction, not weakness, is the approximation.
:::

### Common misconceptions

- **"Weak" means approximate.** No. $(\mathrm S)$ and $(\mathrm W)$ are equivalent at the
  continuous level. The Galerkin restriction is what creates $u^h$.
- **One weighted average is enough.** No. One weight can miss cancellation; the weak form
  requires every $w\in\mathcal V$.
- **A test function is another possible temperature.** Not generally. It is a probe and
  an admissible direction, and it obeys homogeneous essential conditions.
- **$a(w,u)$ is the energy.** Only the quadratic term $\tfrac12 a(u,u)$ is the energy
  term. The two-argument form is its directional cross-term.
- **The Neumann condition was discarded.** It appears in $\ell(w)$ after integration by
  parts. The Dirichlet condition is built into the spaces instead.
- **The heat through the thermostat is lost.** It is not needed to find $u^h$, but it can
  be recovered afterwards from the equation that the thermostat node would have had.
- **Galerkin makes the pointwise residual zero.** Usually not. It makes the residual
  orthogonal to the chosen test space.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## For instructors: a 12-minute in-class sequence
1. **(@sec-wf-conservation, 3 min)** Drag the control volume and point out
   heat out − heat in = heat generated. Set $\kappa_2$ small to show the kink: "The strong
   form can't even be evaluated here."
2. **(@sec-wf-probe, 4 min)** Choose the straight-line guess with the soft control volume
   and sweep the center: "The control volume *is* a test function." Switch to the exact
   solution (every probe reads 0), then to Galerkin with FE hats (all 0), then to Galerkin
   with bumps (not 0).
3. **(@sec-wf-energy, 3 min)** Nudge the exact solution along any direction: a
   flat-bottomed parabola. Then choose "constant 1" to see why $w(1)=0$.
4. **(@sec-wf-bowl, 2 min)** Have a student call out slider moves to find the bottom by
   hand, then press *Snap*: "Each row of $\mathbf K\mathbf d=\mathbf F$ says the bowl is
   flat in one direction."
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your understanding
1. Why must a test function vanish on $\Gamma_g$ but not on $\Gamma_h$? Give a physical
   reason and an energy reason.
2. In the probe explorer with the Galerkin candidate, why do the FE hats read zero while a
   bump of the same width centered *between* two nodes does not?
3. Suppose $\kappa$ were negative somewhere. What happens to the energy parabola, and to
   uniqueness?
4. For the axially loaded rod, restate the table "The weak form, said three ways" with
   "force balance" in place of "heat balance".
:::
